clinicalPearls: An X-linked combined immunodeficiency of males caused by mutations in MSN, which encodes moesin, a protein linking the plasma membrane to the actin cytoskeleton
The characteristic laboratory picture is profound lymphopenia affecting T cells, B cells, and natural killer cells
Presents with recurrent bacterial and viral infections, including varicella-zoster reactivation and other herpesvirus disease
Neutropenia may accompany the lymphopenia, broadening the infective susceptibility
Despite low lymphocyte numbers, some antibody production is retained, and the clinical severity is variable
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating the combined lymphopenia and impaired lymphocyte migration together with MSN sequencing
Management uses immunoglobulin replacement and antimicrobial prophylaxis, with some patients improving over time and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation reserved for severe disease
reference.pathophysiology: Moesin belongs to the ezrin-radixin-moesin family of proteins that tether the cortical actin cytoskeleton to the cell membrane and thereby govern cell shape, membrane dynamics, and movement. In lymphocytes this linkage is required for the cytoskeletal rearrangements underlying migration through tissues, adhesion, and the formation of the immunological synapse during activation. Loss of moesin impairs these processes, so lymphocytes migrate and proliferate poorly and fail to survive in normal numbers, producing a combined lymphopenia of T, B, and natural killer cells. The defective leucocyte trafficking and activation leave the host prone to recurrent bacterial and viral infections, with herpesvirus reactivation reflecting the weakened cellular immunity.
additionalDifferentials: Typical severe combined immunodeficiency of other genetic causes
Other cytoskeletal immune defects such as DOCK2, DOCK8, and coronin-1A deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Lymphocyte subset enumeration showing combined T, B, and natural killer cell lymphopenia
Full blood count to detect associated neutropenia
T-cell proliferation and lymphocyte migration or adhesion assays
Quantitative immunoglobulins and specific antibody responses
Viral studies including varicella-zoster and other herpesviruses
Newborn screening T-cell receptor excision circle results where available
redFlags: Profound combined lymphopenia in a male infant or child
Severe or reactivated herpesvirus infection such as varicella-zoster
Recurrent bacterial infection with accompanying neutropenia
Failure to thrive with early recurrent infection
A maternal family history suggesting X-linked inheritance
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is variable; some patients stabilise or improve on supportive treatment with immunoglobulin replacement and prophylaxis, while those with severe, persistent immunodeficiency may require haematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
pitfalls: Assuming profound lymphopenia always denotes classic severe combined immunodeficiency
Overlooking associated neutropenia as a contributor to infection
Giving live vaccines before the immune defect is excluded
Failing to consider X-linked inheritance in an affected male
Underestimating the variability in severity between patients
references: Stiehm's Immunologic Disorders in Infants and Children
IUIS Expert Committee classification of inborn errors of immunity
management: Provide immunoglobulin replacement therapy to compensate for impaired antibody responses
Give antibacterial prophylaxis and antiviral prophylaxis or treatment for herpesviruses such as varicella-zoster with aciclovir-class agents
Treat intercurrent bacterial and viral infections promptly and aggressively
Consider haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the definitive option in severe, persistent combined immunodeficiency
Avoid live vaccines and use irradiated, leucodepleted blood products given the T-cell defect
Monitor lymphocyte subsets, neutrophil counts and for herpesvirus reactivation
Offer genetic counselling for X-linked inheritance and test at-risk male relatives
